title: When Thai Ferries Cancel: What Actually Happens
content:
Ferries to Thailand's islands get cancelled. Not often, and not everywhere — but when a crossing is suspended, most travelers discover they have no idea what happens next: whether the ticket is refunded, whether they can fly instead, or who is responsible for the connection waiting at the other end. Here is how cancellation actually works, and which of those questions has a good answer.

Who decides

Operators make the call on their own sailings, guided by Marine Department weather warnings and their own assessment of conditions at the pier. The Marine Department — the government body under the Ministry of Transport that oversees maritime safety — can also order suspensions outright.

The practical point is that nobody at your hotel, and no travel agent, can tell you in advance whether tomorrow's boat will run. It is a decision made close to departure by people looking at the sea, and it is not negotiable when it goes against you.

Which crossings are most exposed

Rough conditions do not affect all routes equally. Crossings to Koh Tao and Koh Phangan are the ones most frequently suspended, partly because of the open water involved and partly because of the boats that serve them. The two coasts also have opposite wet seasons, so exposure moves around the calendar rather than applying to the whole country at once — the Gulf islands are most affected roughly October to December, the Andaman side around September and October.

Boat type matters too. Speedboats stop running in conditions that larger ferries will still cross in, so the fast option is also the fragile one.

What happens to your ticket

Booked directly with the operator

Weather cancellations commonly result in a rebooking or a credit rather than a cash refund, and the specifics vary by operator — some tickets are sold non-refundable outright, cancellation or not. This surprises people who expect a weather cancellation to mean their money back. Contractually, it usually means a seat on a later boat.

Where a speedboat is cancelled, the normal outcome is that you are moved onto the same company's slower ferry rather than refunded the difference in price. You paid for speed and you get the crossing.

Combined bus-and-boat or flight-and-boat tickets

This is the one worth understanding before you buy. Combined tickets are convenient and widely sold, and when only the boat leg fails, the onward bus or flight portion is often not covered — the responsibility depends on who sold you the ticket and what their terms say about partial failure.

It is worth reading those terms at the point of purchase rather than at the pier. A ticket that bundles three legs is not automatically a ticket that protects three legs.

Booked through a platform

Aggregator bookings generally follow the underlying operator's policy, with the platform's own cancellation window layered on top. The extra intermediary means an extra link in the chain when you need to reach someone quickly.

Whether you can fly instead

This is the most useful thing to know before you choose an island, and it is entirely knowable in advance. Some islands have an airport. Some do not, and the boat is the only way off.

Air escape availableBoat only
Koh Samui (USM)Koh Tao
Phuket (HKT)Koh Phangan
Krabi (KBV)Koh Lanta

Read those two columns together with the previous section and the shape of the problem appears: Koh Tao and Koh Phangan are both the most cancellation-prone crossings and the islands with no way out except a boat. When a suspension hits, travelers on Samui have options. Travelers on Koh Tao have a wait.

The connection at the other end

Here is the fact most travelers have backwards: a separately booked domestic flight is not protected by your international ticket. If you booked your Bangkok-to-island flight yourself, on a different reservation from the long-haul home, the airline that flies you across the Pacific has no obligation to you when a boat makes you miss it. There is no rebooking, no protection, no through-checking. You buy a new ticket.

Most people assume some invisible safety net exists because their legs are all part of one trip. It does not exist. Two separate bookings are two separate contracts, and weather is nobody's fault, which means it is yours.

Trip interruption cover is the part of a policy that speaks to this, rather than the medical cover most policies lead with — worth checking what your travel insurance says about missed connections caused by weather before you need to find out.

Booking around it

Some things are simply in your control:

  • Take the earlier crossing. If a day's sailings are going to be cancelled, the later ones are likelier to go first, and an early boat leaves room to recover the same day.
  • Prefer the larger ferry when conditions look marginal. It is slower and it crosses in weather that grounds the speedboats.
  • Book the boat leg directly with the operator when that leg is carrying something important, so there is one fewer party between you and the rebooking.
  • Know before you go whether your island has an airport. That single fact determines whether a suspension is an inconvenience or a genuine problem.

Ferry fares vary by route, boat type and season, so check a live figure rather than planning against a fixed one:

Where this decision actually sits

Notice what happened across all of this: almost none of it is really about boats. Which island you can reach, whether it has an airport, which coast you are on in which month, and how your flights are booked are four separate decisions that people make weeks apart — and they only fail together. The travelers who get caught are rarely the ones who picked the wrong ferry. They are the ones whose island, month and departure arrangements were each individually reasonable.

Working out how those four fit together for a specific set of dates is the kind of thing that is easier to read once than to reconstruct from a dozen separate pages, and it is worked out in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

Who decides whether a Thai ferry is cancelled?

The operator makes the call on its own sailings, guided by Marine Department weather warnings and conditions at the pier. The Marine Department can also order suspensions directly. It is decided close to departure, not days ahead.

Do I get a refund if my ferry is cancelled?

Usually not in cash. Weather cancellations commonly result in a rebooking or credit, policies vary by operator, and some tickets are non-refundable regardless. Combined bus-and-boat tickets are the ones to check carefully, since a failed boat leg often does not cover the onward portion.

Which Thai island crossings are cancelled most often?

Crossings to Koh Tao and Koh Phangan are the most frequently suspended. Speedboats stop running in conditions that larger ferries still cross in, so the fast option is the more fragile one.

Can I fly instead if the ferry is cancelled?

Only from islands with an airport — Koh Samui, Phuket and Krabi have one. Koh Tao, Koh Phangan and Koh Lanta do not, so the boat is the only way off.

Will my airline rebook me if a ferry makes me miss my flight?

Not if the flights were booked separately. A separately booked domestic leg has no protection from your international ticket — you would be buying a new one. Trip interruption cover on a travel insurance policy is the thing that speaks to this.
excerpt: Who decides when a crossing is suspended, what happens to your ticket, and which islands let you fly out instead.

title: Thai ATM Fees: What Withdrawing Cash Really Costs
content:
Thailand runs on cash more than most first-time visitors expect, and every ATM withdrawal on a foreign card carries a flat fee that does not shrink when you take out less. That single detail — flat, not percentage — quietly decides how much a two-week trip costs you in fees. It also now depends on which card you put in the machine, which is the part almost nobody checks.

The fee is no longer one number

For years the answer was simple: Thai ATMs charged a flat 220 baht to foreign cards, at every bank, on every withdrawal. That figure is still quoted in most guides, and it is no longer reliably what you will see on the screen.

Thai banks have moved to fees that vary by card network. Visa withdrawals commonly show around 250 baht, while Mastercard withdrawals can show up to 350 baht at the same machine. Some banks still charge 220, and AEON — whose ATMs sit inside Big C and Lotus's supermarkets — is noticeably cheaper at roughly 150.

The practical consequence is easy to miss: if you are carrying both a Visa and a Mastercard, which one you reach for can change the cost of every single withdrawal for the whole trip. Nothing about the machine tells you this in advance. The fee is displayed on screen before you confirm, so the habit worth building is simply reading that screen rather than clicking through it.

Why flat fees change the maths

Because the largest charge is flat, it is the number of withdrawals that costs you, not the amount. Taking out 2,000 baht and taking out 20,000 baht incur exactly the same fee. Someone withdrawing small amounts as they go can easily pay several times what someone withdrawing in larger blocks pays, for exactly the same cash in hand.

The other three charges

The bank's flat fee is the one travelers notice. It is rarely the only one.

Your home bank's foreign transaction fee

Most US cards add their own charge, typically somewhere between nothing and 3% depending on the account. Unlike the Thai fee, this one scales with the amount — so it pushes gently in the opposite direction from the flat fee, though rarely enough to outweigh it.

The network's exchange margin

Visa and Mastercard apply their own spread when converting. It is built into the rate rather than itemised, which is why it tends to go unnoticed even by people who watch fees carefully.

Dynamic currency conversion — the avoidable one

At some point the machine will ask whether you want to be charged in US dollars or in Thai baht. Accepting dollars hands the conversion to the ATM operator, at a rate typically 3-7% worse than the interbank rate your card network would have used. On a large withdrawal that single tap costs more than the flat fee did.

The rule has no exceptions: always choose baht. Decline the conversion offer and let your own card network handle it. The screen is designed to make accepting look like the safe, familiar option — it is the expensive one.

What the cadence actually costs

Put the flat fee against a realistic trip and the spread is larger than most people assume. Take a traveler who needs 60,000 baht in cash across two weeks, at a bank charging the Visa rate:

Withdrawal patternWithdrawalsFlat fees paid
3,000 baht as needed205,000 baht
6,000 baht at a time102,500 baht
20,000 baht at a time3750 baht

Same cash, same trip, same bank — and the careless pattern costs over 4,000 baht more than the deliberate one, before any percentage charges are added. Put a Mastercard in the machine instead of a Visa and every row gets worse again.

The ceiling that caps it

You cannot simply withdraw everything at once. Thai ATMs cap a single transaction at roughly 20,000 to 30,000 baht depending on the bank, so there is a floor under how few withdrawals a trip can involve. That ceiling is what turns "take out more, less often" from vague advice into something with an actual optimum.

There is a counterweight, and it is a real one. Cash you are carrying is cash that can be lost or stolen, and a hotel safe is not always available or trustworthy. The fee arithmetic pushes toward large infrequent withdrawals; sense pushes back. Most travelers land somewhere in the middle rather than at either extreme, and that is the right place to be — the point is to arrive there deliberately rather than by drifting into twenty small withdrawals without noticing.

Ways to pay less

Accounts that refund the fee entirely

A few US accounts reimburse foreign ATM fees, which removes this whole calculation. Charles Schwab's checking account and Fidelity's cash management account are the two most commonly used by American travelers for exactly this reason. If you already hold one, the flat fee stops mattering and you can withdraw as often as you like. If you do not, it is worth knowing they exist before the next trip rather than after this one.

Use the cheaper network, and the cheaper machine

Where you have a choice, Visa currently costs less than Mastercard at most Thai banks, and AEON's machines undercut the major banks by a wide margin. Neither is a dramatic saving on any single withdrawal; across a trip they compound.

How much cash you actually need

Your cash floor is set by where you spend, not by your budget. Street food, markets, tuk-tuks, songthaews, small vendors and most rural businesses are cash-only in practice. Hotels, malls, chain restaurants and upscale places take cards comfortably. A trip weighted toward the first list needs materially more cash on hand than one weighted toward the second — and that, rather than the fee itself, is what should drive how often you visit a machine.

Bringing dollars instead

Exchanging USD cash at a dedicated booth can beat repeated ATM withdrawals for larger sums, once the flat fee is counted. Airport counters are consistently worse than city booths, so the airport is the place to change the minimum you need to get into town rather than your trip's cash. Rates move daily, so check a live figure rather than planning against a fixed one:

100 USD ≈ … THB (enable JavaScript for today's rate)

Where this fits in the trip

The fee arithmetic is simple once you can see it. What makes it awkward in practice is that withdrawal cadence is not really a money decision — it is a routing decision. How much cash you need at once depends on which islands you are on and whether they have bank ATMs, how many days you are away from a city, and whether the next leg is somewhere cards work at all. People end up making twenty small withdrawals not because they miscounted the fee, but because their itinerary never let them plan further ahead than the next two days.

How the cash plan falls out of the route — rather than being bolted on afterwards — is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

How much do Thai ATMs charge foreign cards?

A flat per-withdrawal fee that now varies by card network — commonly around 250 baht on Visa and up to 350 baht on Mastercard, with some banks still at 220 and AEON machines lower at roughly 150. The fee is displayed on screen before you confirm, so check it rather than assuming the old 220 figure.

Should I withdraw large amounts less often?

Mostly yes, because the fee is flat rather than a percentage — twenty small withdrawals can cost several thousand baht more than a handful of large ones. But transactions are capped at roughly 20,000-30,000 baht, and carrying a lot of cash has its own risk, so the sensible answer is fewer, larger withdrawals rather than the largest possible.

Should I choose baht or dollars at the ATM?

Always baht. Accepting the machine's offer to charge you in dollars hands the conversion to the ATM operator at a rate typically 3-7% worse than your card network's. Decline it every time.

Is it cheaper to bring US dollars and exchange them?

For larger sums it can be, once the flat ATM fee is counted, and dedicated city exchange booths give better rates than airport counters. For smaller amounts the convenience of an ATM usually wins.

Can I use cards everywhere in Thailand?

No. Hotels, malls, chain and upscale restaurants take cards, but street food, markets, tuk-tuks, songthaews, small vendors and most rural businesses are cash-only in practice.
excerpt: The flat fee now depends on your card network, and the number of withdrawals matters more than the amount. The full stack, with the arithmetic.

title: Renting a Scooter in Thailand: The Licence and Insurance Chain
content:
Renting a scooter is one of the easiest things to do in Thailand and one of the most common. Vendors hand over a bike for a small daily rate, often without asking for much. The part that catches Americans out is not the riding — it is that the same casual transaction that makes renting easy is what can leave you uninsured if something happens. Here is the actual chain, and what to sort out before you go.

What Thailand legally requires

To ride a motorbike or scooter legally in Thailand you need a valid motorcycle licence from your home country, plus an International Driving Permit. Both, not either.

The International Driving Permit

Thailand recognises the 1949 Geneva Convention permit, which is the standard one issued in the United States. In the US only AAA and AATA are authorised to issue it — anything else offering you an "international licence" online is not the real document.

It costs around $20 plus photo fees. You can walk into a AAA branch and get one the same day, or apply by mail and wait anywhere from about a week upward. That same-day option matters: this is a fixable problem right up until you fly, and an unfixable one afterwards.

The part most people miss

Here is the detail that catches out otherwise careful travelers. An IDP does not grant you anything. It translates the entitlements your home licence already carries into a format Thai authorities can read.

So if your US driver's licence has no motorcycle endorsement — and most do not, because most Americans have never ridden — then your IDP does not add one. You can hold a valid driver's licence, hold a valid IDP, do everything you thought was required, and still not be licensed to ride a scooter. That gap is where insurance claims get denied, and it is invisible unless someone tells you about it.

What actually happens at the rental shop

Very little. Vendors rarely check licence details with any care, and plenty will hand over a bike against a passport photocopy and a cash deposit without asking whether you can legally ride it.

It is worth being clear about what that means: the vendor not checking is not permission. It is simply the reason most people discover the problem after a crash instead of before one. The transaction feels like approval and carries none.

One related trap, covered in more detail in our guide to common scams in Thailand: never leave your actual passport as a deposit. A photocopy or a cash deposit is normal and safe; the original in someone else's drawer is leverage against you in any dispute about damage.

Being stopped versus being hurt

There are two costs here and they are wildly different in size, which is why conflating them leads people astray.

The small one

Police checkpoints are common in tourist areas, and riding without the right permit or without a helmet typically means a fine of a few hundred baht — commonly in the region of 400 to 500. Helmets are legally required for both rider and passenger. Being stopped is an inconvenience and a small expense, and travelers who have been stopped once tend to conclude, reasonably enough, that the whole issue is overblown.

The large one

The fine is not the risk. The risk is that many travel insurance policies exclude motorbike accidents where the rider held no valid motorcycle licence, or was not wearing a helmet — and where the exclusion applies, the insurer can deny the claim in full. Not reduce it. Deny it.

What an uninsured accident costs

Thai private hospitals are excellent and they expect payment. A serious motorbike injury requiring surgery runs into the tens of thousands of US dollars at a private hospital — the kind of number that reshapes a year, not a holiday.

Medical evacuation is the expensive line item on top of that. Getting someone off a small island to Bangkok, or home to the United States with medical support, can cost far more again. It is the specific coverage worth confirming you have, because it is the one people assume is included and often is not.

Two things Americans routinely assume cover them and generally do not: your domestic US health insurance provides little or no coverage abroad and almost never covers evacuation, and credit card travel benefits are usually thinner than a dedicated policy. Our guide to travel insurance for Thailand goes through what a policy should actually include.

Road accidents are the most common serious problem travelers face in Thailand, and motorbikes are overwhelmingly the vehicle involved. That is not a reason to avoid the country; it is a reason to be the person who sorted out the paperwork.

What to sort out before you fly

All of this is cheap and easy to fix in advance, and impossible to fix afterwards:

  • Get the motorcycle endorsement on your home licence if there is any chance you will ride. This is the long-lead item — it may involve a test — and it is the one that actually determines whether you are covered.
  • Get the IDP from AAA or AATA. Same day in person, around $20.
  • Confirm your policy in writing — specifically what it says about motorbike riding, and under what conditions it pays out.
  • Wear the helmet, every time. It is legally required, and it is frequently a condition of the coverage itself.
  • Photograph the bike before you ride away, documenting existing damage.

If you already know you will not ride, none of this applies to you, and that is a perfectly good trip rather than a timid one. The travelers who get caught are almost never the ones who planned to ride. They are the ones who found themselves somewhere the beach was six kilometres away, the songthaews had stopped, and a scooter was obviously the easiest answer — and checking travel insurance terms is something to do before that afternoon rather than after it.

Why this is really an itinerary question

Notice what actually decides this. Not risk appetite — geography. Islands and towns where the beaches, viewpoints and restaurants are spread out are the ones where nearly everyone ends up renting something, whatever they intended when they booked. Places with a walkable centre, or cheap and frequent songthaews, are the ones where a scooter simply never comes up.

Which means whether you will be riding is mostly settled weeks earlier, when you choose where to stay — which is exactly the moment nobody is thinking about licence endorsements. By the time the question is live, the endorsement is no longer obtainable.

Which bases genuinely require wheels and which quietly do not is mapped out in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

Do I need an International Driving Permit to ride a scooter in Thailand?

Yes — Thailand requires a valid motorcycle licence from your home country plus a 1949 Geneva Convention IDP. In the US, only AAA and AATA are authorised to issue one.

Is an IDP enough on its own?

No, and this is the detail that catches people out. An IDP only translates the entitlements your home licence already carries. If your US licence has no motorcycle endorsement, the IDP does not add one — you would be riding unlicensed even holding both documents.

Will rental shops check my licence?

Usually not with any care. But the vendor not checking is not permission, and it has no bearing on whether your insurer pays out if you crash.

Will my travel insurance cover a scooter accident?

It depends entirely on your policy. Many exclude motorbike accidents where the rider had no valid motorcycle licence or no helmet, and can deny the claim in full. Confirm your own policy's wording in writing before you ride rather than assuming.

How much does a motorbike accident cost without insurance?

A serious injury requiring surgery at a Thai private hospital runs into the tens of thousands of US dollars, with medical evacuation costing considerably more again. US domestic health insurance generally will not cover it.
excerpt: An IDP does not add a motorcycle entitlement your home licence lacks — and that gap is where insurance claims get denied.
